# How Much Should a Coffee Shop Spend on Google Ads?

Part of the guide: [Coffee Shop Marketing](https://datalatte.pro/guides/coffee-marketing)

May 16, 2026·Nataliia Rumiantsewa· 9 min read [All posts](https://datalatte.pro/blog)

On this page▼

A coffee shop can start Google Ads at about $300 a month ($10 a day) and should raise it only when tracked calls, direction requests or orders pay back. At the 2026 benchmark for Restaurants & Food, which is the closest published category, $300 buys roughly 146 clicks at $2.05 each, or about 10 leads at $30.57 each. Below about $200 a month you collect too few clicks to learn what works, so treat the first two to three months as a test.

These numbers come from an industry average, not from your shop. Costs depend on your **location**, **competition** and **goals**, so the rest of this guide shows how to set a budget you can defend with your own numbers.

* * *

## The Ideal Coffee Shop Google Ads Budget in 2026

There is no one-size-fits-all number, so start from what a budget buys. The table below divides each monthly budget by the 2026 Restaurants & Food averages: $2.05 per click and $30.57 per lead. It is arithmetic on a category average, so your own cost per click will differ by city and by how many cafés bid on the same searches. Confirm local costs in Google's Keyword Planner.

| Monthly budget | Average daily budget | Clicks at $2.05 | Leads at $30.57 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $200 | about $6.60 | about 98 | about 7 |
| $300 | about $9.90 | about 146 | about 10 |
| $500 | about $16.45 | about 244 | about 16 |
| $1,000 | about $32.90 | about 488 | about 33 |

Here a "lead" is a conversion your account tracks, such as a call, a direction request or an order. Daily figures divide the month by 30.4, the multiplier Google uses for its monthly spending limit.

> Pro tip: start with at least $300 a month. Much less than that often fails to produce enough data to optimize.

$30.57

average cost per lead for Restaurants & Food search ads in 2026, against $66.69 across all industries

Average CPC is $2.05 for the category and $5.42 across all industries. Coffee shops are not reported separately.

WordStream by LocaliQ, Search Advertising Benchmarks 2026

* * *

## 1\. How Much Does Google Ads Cost for a Coffee Shop?

For Restaurants & Food, WordStream by LocaliQ lists an average cost per click of $2.05, a click-through rate of 6.83%, a conversion rate of 8.05% and a cost per lead of $30.57. The all-industry averages are $5.42, 6.64%, 8.18% and $66.69. Food businesses are cheaper per click than most categories, but these are averages across many advertisers, not a quote for your street.

### What Drives Cost?

*   **Competition:** how many nearby cafés and chains advertise on the same searches
*   **Quality Score:** Google rewards relevant ads and landing pages with lower costs
*   **Device:** mobile searches dominate local coffee intent
*   **Time of day:** morning and lunch searches are often more competitive
*   **Your Google Business Profile:** an incomplete listing with few reviews can weaken results, so keep it strong with our [Google Business Profile service](https://datalatte.pro/services/google-business-profile)

### How Does Google Charge Against Your Budget?

You set an average daily budget. On a given day a campaign might spend up to twice that amount, and Google's monthly spending limit is 30.4 times the average daily budget, so a $10 daily budget cannot cost more than $304 in a month. You are not billed above that limit.

* * *

Want a free review of your Google presence?

Send your business name. I reply with a short action plan within 48 hours.

[Get my free audit](https://datalatte.pro/free-audit)

## 2\. How to Set Your Coffee Shop Google Ads Budget

### a. Define Your Goal

*   **In-store visits:** Search campaigns with location extensions, plus a strong Google Business Profile
*   **Online orders or catering:** Search ads pointing to an order page, or Performance Max if you have conversion tracking in place (see our [Performance Max guide](https://datalatte.pro/blog/google-performance-max-for-local-business-complete-guide-2026))
*   **Awareness:** Display or YouTube, but only after search is working

### b. Work Backwards From Value

A simple formula:

1.  Decide how many new regulars you want per month.
2.  Estimate what a regular is worth over a few months (average ticket times visits).
3.  Decide what you can pay for each new customer and still be profitable.
4.  Divide by your expected conversion rate, using your own data once you have it.

Percentage-of-revenue rules vary widely, so treat any such rule as a starting point, not a target.

### c. Start Small, Test, Then Scale

Start at a level you can sustain for 8 to 12 weeks. If tracked results are profitable, raise the budget gradually, for example by 10 to 20 percent at a time, and watch cost per customer as you do.

* * *

## 3\. Example Budget Split for $500 a Month

**Illustration with assumption inputs, not a case study.** Take a mid-sized-city café with $500 a month. At the benchmark $30.57 per lead, that is about 16 leads. Assume 40% of leads become a first-time customer, and assume a new regular spends $7 a visit across 12 visits in three months.

| Step | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leads (benchmark) | $500 / $30.57 | about 16 |
| New customers (assumption: 40%) | 16 x 40% | about 6 |
| Value per new regular (assumption) | $7 x 12 visits | $84 |
| Revenue from new regulars | 6 x $84 | about $504 |
| Spend | monthly budget | $500 |

On these assumptions the ads roughly return their spend in revenue within three months, before the cost of coffee and labour. That is a break-even test, not a profit, so improve targeting, ad copy and the landing page before adding money. You could divide the budget like this:

| Campaign (assumption) | Monthly spend | Goal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Search ads for "coffee near me" style terms | $300 | Drive in-store visits during morning and lunch |
| Search ads for specific offers (catering, breakfast specials) | $100 | Capture higher-value o

# Google AdWords for salons: how to make $3,600 in bookings with $175 in ads

![blogpostimage-e1504104743837.jpg](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5b8e935f4611a044775f2688/1540725990384-DA87KJZNW8ZQATURNUTZ/blogpostimage-e1504104743837.jpg)

Has your salon ever advertised online? If so, was it on Facebook? On Yelp? Groupon?

I can say with almost 100% certainty that you've seen a Google AdWord sometime in the past week. They're the ones that look like this when you search for "best haircut NYC"

![haircutnyc.png](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5b8e935f4611a044775f2688/1539918535897-I7L2BF2JKVC0VU83RBP0/haircutnyc.png)

It's clear that Google ads are very important for local businesses: Google now has the internet's largest ad network in the world. 71% of the ads on the internet are done through Google ([source](https://www.mainstreetroi.com/15-stats-that-prove-google-adwords-is-a-great-investment-for-your-business/)).

So it seems like a ton of businesses are advertising on Google, but how much money are they actually making? On average, businesses make $2 for every $1 they spend on AdWords ([source](https://www.mainstreetroi.com/15-stats-that-prove-google-adwords-is-a-great-investment-for-your-business/)).  

#   
This is why your salon should start advertising with AdWords

  
Here are a few more stats that will help you understand why your salon needs to get going with ads:

72% of your potential clients prefer to find information about local businesses like yours via search ([source](https://www.mainstreetroi.com/15-stats-that-prove-google-adwords-is-a-great-investment-for-your-business/)). Google is their main source of info to learn about salons in your city.

However (and this is the potential downside) 98% of those searchers choose a business that is on page 1 of the results they get.

Does your salon appear on the first page of Google when people search “balayage" or "best eyebrow waxing" in your city? If not, you might be out of luck.

But with the right setup, in AdWords you can easily target the exact searches you want. So you can target people searching for “Hair Extensions”, and give them an ad about Hair Extensions.

And the real magic of Adwords is that you’re reaching people who you don’t need to even need to “sell” to very hard. They’re already searching for the best eyelash extensions or rainbow hair or couple's massage in their city.

This is one of the biggest differences between Adwords and Facebook ads, which many beauty businesses are experimenting with. AdWords is more active whereas Facebook is more passive. This means that with Facebook you need to create great copy, find the right images, the right message, and even the right offer to get someone to commit to your business.

With Adwords, you're talking to people who are already half-committed to make an appointment.

So what makes for a good Google advertisement for salons? It just comes down making sure you give potential clients a good offer and a fast way to get it.  

#   
How to generate $3,600 in revenue through for your salon, spending less than $200

  
I chatted with Robert Norberciak, who is the owner of [Mozaik Skin & Body](https://www.mozaikskin.com/) in Scottsdale, Arizona. He bought the day spa a few years ago and took it from $5,800/mo to $70,000/mo in just a few years.

Yes, you read that right. $70,000 per month. In just a few years.

How did he grow it so much, so fast? Robert’s secret weapon has been Google Adwords (it’s no coincidence that Robert also owns [Maya Media](http://mayamedia.io/), which specializes in Google Adwords campaigns).

Let’s look specifically at one of his campaigns, targeted towards people in his area who are searching for a couples massage on Google.

![Screen-Shot-2017-08-03-at-4.50.48-PM.png](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5b8e935f4611a044775f2688/1539918533273-2VYIFPPPC2F6PWOG80AD/Screen-Shot-2017-08-03-at-4.50.48-PM.png)

Upon searching for something like "couples massage Scottsdale", people will see a simple Google Ad for an offer at Mozaik. Clicking on it, the searcher will see a page like this:     This is called a “landing page” because it’s a simplified page just for this offer. You’ll notice that it is very simple: it doesn’t have a menu and the focus is on “Book Now”. It only talks about a couples massage.

What kind of results has Robert gotten from this ad? You might be a little blown away by this…

**Clicks on the ad from Google:** 92 **Total cost:** $175 **Total conversions** (how many people booked an appointment): 31 (34%) **Revenue Generated:** $3,689 (31 people who spent $119 each)

I don’t know about you, but I am just amazed these numbers. Each new booking cost him  just $5.60, with a value of $119. Insane.

So, you want to have the same success for your next ad campaign? Read on...  

#   
Step 1: Choose an offer and build a landing page for it

  
Remember the landing page that Robert set up for Mozaik? It was focused on just one service, just one offer.

Some of the specific services you can focus on are:

*   Couples massage
    
*   Microblading
    
*   Spray tans for weddings
    
*   Hair extensions
    
*   Bikini waxing
    
*   Rainbow hair
    

In short, your best bet for a successful campaign is to focus on something you do really well. Something specific that people are searching for.

Now that you’ve chosen your offer, time to build a landing page!

You can actually create really simple and easy landing pages with my favourite website, [Instapage](http://www.instapage.com/).

![instapage2.png](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5b8e935f4611a044775f2688/1539918536071-7C4JINZ9BHS00NQW20TJ/instapage2.png)

Check out these examples of beautiful landing page templates they have:  

![Screen-Shot-2017-08-03-at-4.41.24-PM-1.png](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5b8e935f4611a044775f2688/1539918532379-U3XJ4TVXXJZ46Y9PFF3S/Screen-Shot-2017-08-03-at-4.41.24-PM-1.png)

![instapage4.png](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5b8e935f4611a044775f2688/1539918536877-L9C9GKD5OS8LHHNA7TT2/instapage4.png)

  What should your landing page have on it?

###   
1) No menu links except for your call to action 

###   
2) A “call to action” to EASILY book an appointment or claim your offer

  
This is the button people have to click on your landing page.

# What Does a Salon Booking Cost on Google Ads? Real Numbers From One Salon

![What a salon booking really costs: $5.40 per booking action at a NYC salon spending $1.6K a month](https://arccreativeco.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/salon-booking-cost-google-ads.jpg)

_By Adam Cortez, founder of ARC Creative Co. Built from the numbers in our own client accounts, linked below._

Short answer

In one New York salon account, Google Ads cost **$5.40 per booking action** (a booking-widget open or a call over 60 seconds) on $1.6K a month. That’s not the same as cost per booked appointment: divide the cost per action by the share of actions that become bookings. If 1 in 2 becomes a booking, an appointment costs about $10.80. Whether that’s good depends on what a new client is worth to you.

## The real numbers from one salon

| Measure | NYC blowout and makeup salon |
| --- | --- |
| Period | April 18 – May 17, 2023 |
| Google Ads spend | $1.6K |
| Clicks | 615 |
| Booking actions (widget opens + calls over 60 seconds) | 296 |
| **Cost per booking action** | **$5.40** |
| Facebook/Instagram cost per click, 1–2 mile radius | $1.19 and $1.37 |
| Appointments from Meta retargeting, 30 days | 53  |

From ARC’s [salon case study](https://arccreativeco.com/case-studies/salon-case-study/). One salon in one market; yours will differ.

Treat this as a real reference point, not a benchmark. New York is an expensive ad market, and blowouts and makeup are frequent, lower-ticket services. Extensions, color correction or bridal work will cost more per booking and are worth more per client.

## How to work out your own cost per booking

1.  **Cost per booking action** = ad spend ÷ tracked actions. Google Ads shows this as cost per conversion.
2.  **Booking rate** = new-client bookings in your booking software ÷ tracked actions, for the same month.
3.  **Cost per booked appointment** = cost per booking action ÷ booking rate.

**Example (illustrative):** at $5.40 per action and a 50% booking rate, each booked appointment costs $10.80. At a 25% booking rate it costs $21.60. You only know your rate if your tracking is honest; see [how to track salon bookings when your software doesn’t connect to Google Analytics](https://arccreativeco.com/track-salon-bookings-from-google-ads/).

## How much can you afford to pay?

Work from what a new client brings in, not one visit. If a new client spends $80 a visit and books three more times in a year, they’re worth $320 in revenue that year. Decide what share of that you’re willing to spend to win them; that is your ceiling cost per booked appointment. Most salons find Google Ads affordable once they measure bookings rather than clicks.

## What makes a salon booking cheaper or more expensive

*   **Market:** dense cities cost more per click than suburbs and small towns.
*   **Service:** high-ticket services attract more competing advertisers.
*   **Radius:** a tight radius around the salon wastes less money on people who won’t travel.
*   **Branded vs. new clients:** people searching your salon’s name are cheap. Report them separately or they’ll flatter the numbers.
*   **Follow-up:** retargeting on Facebook and Instagram turns visitors who didn’t book into appointments. It produced 53 in 30 days for this salon.

## Questions salon and practice owners ask

### How much does Google Ads cost for a salon?

In one New York salon account, $1.6K a month produced 296 booking actions at $5.40 each. Your cost depends on your market, services and how you track bookings.

### What is a good cost per booking for a salon?

One you can afford given what a new client is worth over a year. Work out cost per booked appointment, not cost per click, and compare it to that value.

### Should a salon use Google Ads or Instagram ads?

Both do different jobs. Google Ads reaches people already searching for your service; Facebook and Instagram can target people within a mile or two of the salon and retarget visitors who didn’t book.

results.title: About Quality Score for Search campaigns
results.markdown:
Title: About Quality Score for Search campaigns

URL Source: https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6167118

Markdown Content:
Quality Score is a diagnostic tool meant to give you a sense of how well your [ad quality](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/156066) compares to other advertisers.

This score is measured on a scale from 1-10 and available at the keyword level. A higher Quality Score means that your ad and landing page are more relevant and useful to someone searching for your keyword, compared to other advertisers.

You can use the Quality Score diagnostic tool to identify where it might be beneficial to improve your ads, landing pages, or keyword selection.

**On this page**

*   [Calculate Quality Score](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6167118#calculate_score)
*   [Check Quality Score](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6167118#check_qs)

**Good to know about Quality Score**

*   Quality Score is not a key performance indicator and should not be optimized or aggregated with the rest of your data.
*   Quality Score is not an input in the ad auction. It’s a diagnostic tool to identify how ads that show for certain keywords affect the user experience.

* * *

## [](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6167118)How it’s calculated

Quality Score is calculated based on the combined performance of 3 components:

*   **Expected clickthrough rate (CTR)**: The likelihood that your ad will be clicked when shown.
*   **Ad relevance**: How closely your ad matches the intent behind a user's search.
*   **Landing page experience**: How relevant and useful your landing page is to people who click your ad.

Each component is evaluated with a status of “Above average,” “Average,” or “Below average.” This evaluation is based on a comparison with other advertisers whose ads showed for the exact same search over the last 90 days.

A broad match keyword may have a Quality Score even though it has no impressions as long as there is a corresponding exact match keyword with impressions in the last 90 days. If there are impressions for searches that exactly match a broad match keyword through an exact match keyword in the same ad group, this will report the same Quality Score for both of the keywords.

If one of these components has a status of “Average” or “Below average”, this may indicate an opportunity to make improvements. Learn more about [5 ways to use Quality Score to improve your performance](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6167130).

### Keep in mind

*   Quality Score is based on **historical impressions for exact searches**of your keyword, therefore changing keyword match types will not impact Quality Score.
*   If you notice a “—” in the Quality Score column, it means there aren't enough searches that exactly match your keywords to determine a keyword’s Quality Score. To help gather traffic data and resolve this status: 
    *   **Use Keyword Planner to discover higher-volume keywords:** Identify relevant search terms with sufficient search volume.
    *   **Broaden match types:** While match types don't change how your Quality Score is calculated, broadening them helps your keyword participate in more auctions, increasing the chances of gathering enough exact-match search data to generate a score.

*   There are factors related to your ad quality that might not be captured by Quality Score. These factors include, but are not limited to: 
    *   Devices used in search
    *   Location of user
    *   Time of day
    *   Assets

*   Information obtained from any of Google's various [crawlers](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/advanced/crawling/overview-google-crawlers)may be used to assess ad quality, which can be reflected through Quality Score.

* * *

## [](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6167118)How to check your Quality Score

1.   Go to [**Keywords**](https://ads.google.com/aw/keywords) within the **Campaigns** menu ![Image 1: Campaigns Icon](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/PYU3UjHzepAdY-dWS9ObIzq9WgLGS0SZeJS1hQ0Be3fxCIUQZaWCrR4HoYqriXSEbQ=w40).
2.   In the upper right corner of the table, select the columns icon ![Image 2: A picture of the Google Ads columns icon](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/poJPSxxmyG5nyGxTbdiUmvgDuTZF5IHNddHCp2_gGuax6_nG4coJefjn7KKwJfWu4c8=w50) .
3.   Under “Modify columns for keywords”, select the drop-down arrow beside “All columns” and open the Quality score section.
4.   To add the current Quality Score and its component statuses as new columns in the keyword reporting table, select any of the following: 
    *   Quality Score
    *   Landing Page Exp.
    *   Exp. CTR
    *   Ad Relevance

5.   To view past Quality Score stats for the reporting period you’re looking at, choose any of the following metrics. To add past Quality Score data and its component statuses as new columns in the keyword reporting table, select the following: 
    *   Quality Score (hist.)
    *   Landing Page Exper. (hist.)
    *   Ad Relevance (hist.)
    *   Exp. CTR. (hist.) You can view the change in daily scores by segmenting your table by day. 

6.   Select **Apply**.

* * *

### Related links

*   [5 ways to use Quality Score to improve your performance](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6167130)
*   [About ad quality](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/156066)

### [What Barbers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists Do](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-2)

Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists provide haircutting, hairstyling, and other services related to personal appearance.

### [Work Environment](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-3)

Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists work mostly in barbershops or salons. Most are full time, although part-time work is common. Work schedules may vary and often include evenings and weekends.

### [How to Become a Barber, Hairstylist, or Cosmetologist](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-4)

All states require barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists to be licensed. To qualify for a license, candidates typically must graduate from a state-approved barber or cosmetology program and pass an exam.

### [Pay](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-5)

The median hourly wage for barbers was $18.37 in May 2025.

The median hourly wage for hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists was $17.21 in May 2025.

### [Job Outlook](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-6)

Overall employment of barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists is projected to grow 7 percent from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the average for all occupations.

About 80,300 openings for barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are projected each year, on average, over the decade. Many of those openings are expected to result from the need to replace workers who transfer to different occupations or exit the labor force, such as to retire.

## What Barbers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists Do[About this section](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#TB_inline?height=325&width=325&inlineId=about-what-they-do)

![Image 1: Barbers, hairdressers, and cosmetologists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/images/2711.jpg)

Hairstylists provide hair styling and beauty services.

Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists provide haircutting, hairstyling, and other services related to personal appearance.

### Duties

Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists typically do the following:

*   Inspect and analyze hair, scalp, and skin to recommend services or treatment
*   Discuss hairstyle options
*   Shampoo, color, lighten, and condition hair
*   Chemically change hair texture
*   Cut, dry, and style hair
*   Trim facial hair
*   Receive payments from client
*   Clean and disinfect all tools and work areas

Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists provide hair and other services to enhance clients’ appearance. Common tools may include combs and hairbrushes, clippers and scissors, straight razors, blow dryers, and curling and flat irons. They also may keep records of products used and services provided to clients, such as hair color, hair treatment, and clipper setting.
